title: The Precious Metal Quandary
gist: Central bank gold buying of over 1,000 tonnes a year between 2023 and 2025 — roughly a third of the ~3,500-3,700 tonne annual global production — was triggered by the West's seizure of Russian central bank reserves and drove the precious metals bull market; but the Iran-US/Israel war broke the reflex, with gold falling US$1,200 an ounce and silver and platinum roughly halving from their January 2026 peaks.

themes.theme: Reserve-asset regime shift after Russian asset seizure

insights.claim: The Western decision to seize the Russian central bank's reserves and freeze Russian billionaires' assets at the start of the Russia-Ukraine war ended OECD government bonds' status as the default store-of-value reserve asset for non-Western countries and accelerated the gold bull market.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: The bid for gold is a structural sanctions-risk hedge by non-Western reserve managers, not a cyclical trade — it persists as long as the confiscation precedent stands.
insights.quote: Suddenly, OECD government bonds stopped being the default “store of value” reserve asset for non-Western countries.
insights.locator: The start of the Russia-Ukraine war

insights.claim: Central banks as a group flipped from being marginal sellers of gold to massive buyers, purchasing more than a thousand tonnes each year between 2023 and 2025.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Track quarterly official-sector gold purchase data — a slowdown below the ~1,000 tonne run-rate removes the largest source of marginal demand underpinning the price.
insights.quote: Between 2023 and 2025, central banks as a group purchased more than a thousand tonnes of gold each year.

insights.claim: Annual global gold production hovers around 3,500-3,700 tonnes, meaning official-sector buying of over a thousand tonnes a year absorbed close to a third of new supply in a price-insensitive way.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Sizing marginal demand against fixed mine supply is the cleanest way to judge how much of the gold move is structural versus speculative, and how much downside there is if the buyer steps back.

insights.claim: Investors reflexively assumed the Iran-US/Israel war would push more money into gold, but gold prices instead promptly fell by US$1,200 an ounce.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Geopolitical escalation is no longer a reliable long-gold catalyst; buying conflict headlines in bullion has become a losing reflex worth fading.
insights.quote: the initial gut reaction of many investors was to assume that another war would equate to even more money flowing into gold. Instead, gold prices promptly lost US$1,200 an ounce

insights.claim: Silver and platinum prices have roughly halved since their January 2026 peaks, a more brutal decline than gold's.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: The higher-beta precious metals took the larger drawdown, so any re-entry into the complex should be sized for that leverage — and miners levered to silver/platinum carry the same asymmetry.
insights.quote: The declines in silver and platinum (the prices in both metals have roughly halved since their January 2026 peaks) have been even more brutal
insights.locator: The declines in silver and platinum

insights.claim: The precious metals complex now presents a quandary in which the structural, sanctions-driven central bank bid coexists with a sharp price collapse across gold, silver and platinum, implying the drivers of the bull market and the drivers of the recent drawdown are different forces.
insights.speaker: Gavekal Research
insights.so_what: Separate the official-sector structural bid from speculative war-premium flows when judging whether this drawdown is a buying opportunity or the start of a longer unwind.
